questions.prompt: Patricia says of the childminder: "I felt she was having precious hours with him which should have been mine." What does should have been tell you?

options.text: That the hours will be hers next year.
That she advises other working mothers to keep those hours for themselves.
That the hours ought to have been hers, and were not.
That she is not sure who had those hours.

questions.explanation: should have followed by a past participle names something that ought to have happened and did not, which is exactly Patricia's situation: the hours went to the childminder and cannot be given back. Nothing in the form points forward, so a reading about next year misses it entirely — a plan would be will have or is going to have. It is not advice either: advice is only useful while there is still time to act, and the whole point of this form is that the time has gone. And it says nothing about the speaker's certainty; Patricia knows perfectly well who had those hours, which is precisely why she minds.

questions.prompt: Heidrun explains that the assistant does the small acts of the surgery "so that the doctor does not have to do them". Why does the sentence use so that rather than to?

options.text: Because the two halves have different subjects.
Because so that is more polite than to.
Because the sentence is written in the present tense throughout.
Because the purpose is negative.

questions.explanation: The assistant performs the action and the doctor receives the benefit, so two different people are involved; to plus a verb can only be used when the same person acts in both halves, which is why the sentence needs a full clause and therefore so that. Politeness plays no part: the three structures differ in grammar, not in register, and in order to is the formal one in any case. The tense is irrelevant, since so that works in every tense, as does to. And a negative purpose changes nothing either — you can perfectly well write to avoid disturbing him, with a single subject and no so that in sight.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses used to correctly?

options.text: Modern trains didn't used to exist.
Modern trains didn't use to exist.
Modern trains not used to exist.
Modern trains didn't used exist.

questions.explanation: After did, every verb goes back to its base form, and use is no exception: the d that the affirmative carries is already contained in didn't, so writing it twice is the most frequent mistake of the chapter. That is what rules out didn't used to, however natural it looks on the page. Building the negative without did at all is not English for this verb, since use to is not a modal and cannot take not directly. And dropping the word to breaks the structure itself, because used to is always followed by to plus the base verb.

questions.prompt: Emma Hutchinson wears a hearing aid in each ear and learned to find the right pitch by practising for hours. How does the text describe her deafness?

options.text: She became deaf after an illness.
She is profoundly deaf.
She lost her hearing while studying music.
She was born partially deaf.

questions.explanation: The first line of her story says she was born partially deaf and wears a hearing aid in each ear, and the word partially is what makes the rest possible: she hears something, and the work of her childhood was learning to use it. Profoundly deaf appears in the lesson only as the wrong answer in a vocabulary exercise, and it contradicts the text. Nothing suggests an illness, and nothing suggests a loss at all — she has had the condition since birth, so a story of losing her hearing later, during her studies or otherwise, reverses the order of her life.

questions.prompt: Say these four words aloud and listen to what the final -s does: check-ups, stitches, schools, streets. In which one is the ending pronounced /ɪz/?

options.text: stitches
check-ups
schools
streets

questions.explanation: The sound before the ending in stitches is the hiss of ch, and English cannot add either /s/ or /z/ straight onto a hiss without a vowel in between — that vowel is what makes /ɪz/, and it is the only reason the third sound exists. check-ups and streets both end in the voiceless consonant p or t, where the throat does not vibrate, so they take /s/. schools ends in a voiced l, where it does, so it takes /z/. The pair to watch is stitches and streets: both contain a t, but only stitches puts a hiss immediately before the ending.
